publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CXLV, complete), and on the Protestant doctrine of that distinction, the Lutherans of the Augsburg Confession, the Remonstrants, and the Reformed who subscribe to Dort (I-XLIX). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XXXVI. Praeter Remonstrantes autem, ex Reformatis qui subscribunt Synodo Dordracenae nonnulli quoque gratiam distinguunt in sufficientem atque efficacem, sensu tamen non parum diverso. Quippe hac distinctione utitur Paulus Testardus, dum viveret Pastor Ecclesiae Blaesensis, in Irenico thesi trecentesima, & in libro de Natura & Gratia pluribus in locis. Sed per gratiam sufficientem intelligit illam ipsam quam universalem vocat, per gratiam autem efficacem, eam quam nominat particularem.
english: Thesis XXXVI. Apart from the Remonstrants, some of the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort also divide grace into sufficient and efficacious, though in a quite different sense. Paulus Testardus, pastor of the church at Blois in his lifetime, uses this distinction in his Irenicum, thesis 300, and in many places in his book on nature and grace.
By sufficient grace, however, he means what he calls universal grace, and by efficacious grace what he names particular grace.

source_text: XXXVII. Itaque, ex ejus mente, gratia ista sufficiens non est gratia aliqua subjectiva, quae hominem intus disponat ad fidem & resipiscentiam: sed tantum gratia quaedam objectiva, quae in eo consistit quod salus homini possibilis redditur, tum per Christi satisfactionem, quae sustulit obstaculum illud quod justitia divina opponebat, ne homines peccatorum veniam impetrarent: tum per externam Dei vocationem, & invitationem ad fidem & resipiscentiam, sive per verbum praedicationis, sive per opera naturae & providentiae.
english: Thesis XXXVII. In his view, then, this sufficient grace is not a subjective grace that inwardly disposes a person to faith and repentance. It is only an objective grace, which consists in salvation being made possible for a person.

This happens in two ways: through Christ's satisfaction, which took away the barrier that divine justice set against people obtaining forgiveness of sins, and through God's outward call and invitation to faith and repentance, given either by the preached word or by the works of nature and providence.

source_text: XXXVIII. Gratiam autem illam dicit esse sufficientem, quoniam dat homini posse servari si velit: adeo ut si homo salutis particeps non fiat, stet tantum penes ejus pravitatem & malignitatem, neque de Deo queri possit, quasi aliquid ipsi denegaverit, sine quo absolute non possit esse salvus: cum habeat objectum in sufficienti lumine propositum, & mentem & voluntatem, quae per se possint & debeant illud amplecti atque suscipere: ac quominus id fiat, obstet sola ejus perversitas, cujus ipse causa est, ac propter quam nullam habet rationem de Deo querendi.
english: Thesis XXXVIII. He calls that grace sufficient because it gives a person the ability to be saved if he wills. So if someone does not come to share in salvation, the cause lies only in his own depravity and malice, and he cannot complain of God as though God had denied him something without which he simply could not be saved.

For he has the object set before him in sufficient light, and he has a mind and will that of themselves can and should embrace and accept it. Only his own perversity, of which he himself is the cause, prevents this, and for that reason he has no ground to complain of God.

source_text: XXXIX. Agnoscit tamen ille nunquam contingere posse ut, si non aliud accedat, aliquis per solam istam sufficientem gratiam salvetur: idque propter nativam hominis pravitatem atque improbitatem, quae impedit ne bene utatur mediis illis a Deo propositis, & alioquin in se ad salutem sufficientibus. Et sic fidem & resipiscentiam, ad quas homo sufficienter facultatibus Physicis instructus est, moraliter illi impossibilem reddit. Unde emergit necessitas particularis alicujus gratiae, quae pravitatem hominis corrigat, & ita mentem atque voluntatem intus disponat atque afficiat, ut excussis pravis habitibus, salutem extrinsecus oblatam amplectatur, & fide atque resipiscentia ad misericordiam divinam confugiat, quam gratiam particularem ideo vocat efficacem.
english: Thesis XXXIX. He admits, though, that unless something more is added, no one can ever be saved by this sufficient grace alone. The reason is man's inborn depravity and wickedness, which keeps him from making good use of the means God sets before him, means otherwise sufficient for salvation in themselves.

So that depravity makes faith and repentance morally impossible for him, although his physical faculties equip him adequately for them. Hence the need for a particular grace to correct man's depravity and so to dispose and move his mind and will from within that, once his corrupt habits are shaken off, he embraces the salvation offered from outside and takes refuge in God's mercy by faith and repentance. This particular grace Testard therefore calls efficacious.

source_text: XL. Verum alii Reformati gratiae distinctionem in sufficientem atque efficacem communiter repudiant. Quippe censent nullam gratiam revera sufficientem esse & dici posse, quae etiam non sit efficax. Idque quia ut homo reapse convertatur, requiritur tale Dei auxilium, quo non simpliciter ad bonum moveatur & alliciatur, sed quo voluntas ejus flectatur & determinetur, ut bonum velit & illi adhaereat, absque quo nunquam foret, ut eo ferretur voluntas, obstante ingenita hominis pravitate.
english: Thesis XL. Other Reformed theologians, however, generally reject the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious. In their judgment no grace is really sufficient, or can be called so, unless it is also efficacious.

Their reason is that for a person to be actually converted, God must give a help that does more than simply move and draw him toward the good: it must bend and determine his will to will the good and hold to it. Without such help the will would never be carried there, since man's inborn depravity blocks the way.

source_text: XLI. Etenim communis est Reformatorum omnium, qui Dordracenam Synodum sequuntur, sententia, gratiam Dei, cui tribuenda est hominis conversio, & omnia quae eam subsequuntur bona opera, esse efficacem per se, nec ejus efficaciam ullo modo pendere a cooperatione, sive consensu voluntatis humanae, cum causa sit infallibilis istius consensus, sive cooperationis. Idque congruenter decretis istius Synodi. Siquidem in rejectione errorum circa tertium & quartum articulum Canone 8. damnat eos qui docent Deum in hominis regeneratione eas suae omnipotentiae vires non adhibere, quibus voluntatem ejus ad fidem & conversionem potenter & infallibiliter flectat: sed positis omnibus gratiae operationibus, quibus Deus ad hominem convertendum utitur, hominem tamen Deo, & spiritui regenerationem ejus intendenti, & regenerare ipsum volenti, ita posse resistere, & actu ipso saepe resistere, ut sui regenerationem prorsus impediat, adeoque in ipsius manere potestate, ut regeneretur, vel non regeneretur. Canone vero nono damnat eos quoque qui docent, Gratiam & liberum arbitrium esse causas partiales simul concurrentes ad conversionis initium; nec gratiam ordine causalitatis, efficientiam voluntatis antecedere: Id est, Deum non prius hominis voluntatem efficaciter juvare ad conversionem, quam voluntas ipsa hominis se moveat ac determinet.
english: Thesis XLI. All the Reformed who follow the Synod of Dort hold in common that the grace of God, to which man's conversion and all the good works that follow it must be credited, is efficacious of itself. Its efficacy in no way depends on the cooperation or consent of the human will, since grace itself causes that infallible consent or cooperation.

This agrees with the decrees of that Synod. In the rejection of errors on the third and fourth articles, canon 8, it condemns those who teach 'that in regenerating a person God does not use those powers of his omnipotence by which he would bend the person's will to faith and conversion with power and without fail; but that, with every working of grace that God uses for converting a person in place, the person can still resist God and the Spirit who intends and wills to regenerate him, and often actually does, so as to prevent his own regeneration entirely, and so it remains in his own power whether he is regenerated or not.'

In canon 9 it also condemns those who teach 'that grace and free choice are partial causes acting together at the start of conversion, and that grace does not come before the will's own working in the order of causes'; that is, 'that God does not effectively help a person's will toward conversion before that will moves and determines itself.'

source_text: XLII. Quomodo autem Deus in Electis veram conversionem operetur, sic explicat eadem Synodus, Non tantum, inquit, evangelium illis externe praedicari curat, & mentem eorum per Spiritum Sanctum potenter illuminat, ut recte intelligant & dijudicent quae sunt Spiritus Dei; sed ejusdem etiam spiritus regenerantis efficacia ad intima hominis penetrat, cor clausum aperit, durum emollit, praeputiatum circumcidit, voluntati novas qualitates infundit, facitque eam ex mortua vivam, ex mala bonam, ex nolente volentem, ex refractaria morigeram, agitque & roborat eam, ut ceu arbor bona fructus bonarum actionum proferre possit. In capite doctrinae de hominis corruptione & conversione, ejusque modo articulo undecimo.
english: Thesis XLII. The same Synod explains how God works true conversion in the elect: 'He not only has the gospel preached to them outwardly and powerfully enlightens their minds by the Holy Spirit, so that they rightly understand and judge the things of the Spirit of God.

By the power of the same regenerating Spirit he also reaches into the innermost being of a person: he opens the closed heart, softens the hard one, circumcises the uncircumcised, and pours new qualities into the will. He makes the will alive where it was dead, good where it was bad, willing where it was unwilling, obedient where it was stubborn, and he moves and strengthens it so that, like a good tree, it can bear the fruit of good actions.' This is in the head of doctrine on man's corruption and conversion and its manner, article 11.

source_text: XLIII. Articulo vero sequenti addit eam Dei operationem esse plane supernaturalem, potentissimam simul & suavissimam, mirabilem, arcanam & ineffabilem, virtute sua nec creatione, nec mortuorum resuscitatione minorem aut inferiorem: adeo ut omnes illi, in quorum cordibus admirando hoc modo Deus operatur, certo, infallibiliter & efficaciter regenerentur, & actu credant.
english: Thesis XLIII. In the next article the Synod adds that this working of God is wholly supernatural, both most powerful and most gentle, wonderful, hidden and beyond words, and no less in power than creation or the raising of the dead. So all in whose hearts God works in this wonderful way are regenerated surely, infallibly and effectively, and actually believe.

source_text: XLIV. Proinde cum illa Dei operatio in iis sese non exerat qui reipsa non credunt & poenitentiam agunt, idcirco qui isti Synodo subscribunt Theologi, negant illis gratiam sufficientem dari, quantumcunque externa verbi praedicatione ad poenitentiam & fidem invitentur, & quibusdam etiam internis Spiritus Sancti motibus percellantur.
english: Thesis XLIV. Since that working of God does not show itself in those who do not actually believe and repent, the theologians who subscribe to that Synod deny that such people are given sufficient grace, however much the outward preaching of the word invites them to repentance and faith, and even though some inward motions of the Holy Spirit stir them.

source_text: XLV. Est enim observandum Reformatos qui negant omnes eos qui non convertuntur gratiam ad conversionem sufficientem habere, non negare tamen quin aliquousque gratia Dei operetur in multis qui sese in peccatis obfirmant, nec ad Deum per fidem & resipiscentiam accedunt. Sunt enim, ex eorum mente, quaedam ad conversionem sive regenerationem praevia, quae communia sunt Electis & reprobis, & virtute verbi spiritusque, tam in horum quam in illorum cordibus excitantur. Qualia sunt notitia voluntatis divinae, sensus peccati, timor poenae, cogitatio de liberatione, spes aliqua veniae, aliique motus similes.
english: Thesis XLV. Note that the Reformed who deny that everyone who is not converted has grace sufficient for conversion do not deny that God's grace works to some degree in many who harden themselves in their sins and do not come to God by faith and repentance.

In their view there are certain things that go before conversion or regeneration, common to the elect and the reprobate, which the power of the word and Spirit rouses in the hearts of both alike: knowledge of God's will, a sense of sin, fear of punishment, thoughts of deliverance, some hope of pardon, and other motions of that kind.

source_text: XLVI. Fatentur multos, quos Deus eo modo vocat ad fidem & conversionem, nolle Deum vocantem sequi, & Spiritui Sancto quae ad salutem eorum faciunt suggerenti resistere, ac tandem motus illos per verbum & Spiritum Sanctum in iis excitatos penitus extinguere, & sic propria culpa in aeternum perire.
english: Thesis XLVI. They admit that many whom God calls to faith and conversion in this way refuse to follow God's call, resist the Holy Spirit as he prompts them toward what makes for their salvation, and in the end entirely stifle the motions that the word and the Holy Spirit stirred in them, and so are lost for ever through their own fault.

source_text: XLVII. Haec est inter alios Theologorum Britannorum doctrina, actis Synodi Dordrechtanae inserta. Exponentes enim suam sententiam de articulis tertio & quarto, & agentes de iis quae ad conversionem sunt antecedanea, sic ea de re statuunt thesi secunda & sequentibus, Sunt quaedam effecta interna ad conversionem, sive regenerationem praevia, quae virtute verbi, spiritusque in nondum justificatorum cordibus excitantur; qualia sunt notitia voluntatis divinae, sensus peccati, timor poenae, cogitatio de liberatione, spes aliqua veniae. Quos Deus mediante verbo per spiritum suum hunc in modum afficit, eos ad fidem conversionemque vere, & serio vocat & invitat. Quos ita afficit Deus non deserit nec desistit in vera ad conversionem via promovere, priusquam ab illis per neglectionem voluntariam, aut hujus gratiae initialis repulsam, deseratur.
english: Thesis XLVII. Among others, this is the teaching of the British theologians, included in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. Setting out their opinion on the third and fourth articles and dealing with what comes before conversion, they state in their second thesis and those that follow:

'There are certain inward effects that go before conversion or regeneration, which the power of the word and the Spirit rouses in the hearts of people not yet justified, such as knowledge of God's will, a sense of sin, fear of punishment, thoughts of deliverance, and some hope of pardon. Those whom God moves in this way by his Spirit, through the word, he calls and invites to faith and conversion truly and in earnest.
Those whom God so moves he does not abandon, nor does he stop leading them forward on the true road to conversion, until they abandon him by wilful neglect or by refusing this initial grace.'

source_text: XLVIII. Hi praecedanei effectus, virtute verbi spiritusque in hominum mentibus producti, rebellis voluntatis vitio, suffocari ac penitus extingui possunt, & in multis solent; adeo ut nonnulli in quorum mentibus virtute verbi spiritusque impressa fuit aliqualis notitia veritatis divinae, aliqualis dolor de peccatis suis, aliquod desiderium & aliqua cura liberationis, mutentur plane in contrarium, veritatem rejiciant & odio habeant, concupiscentiis suis se tradant, in peccatis occalleant, & absque desiderio vel cura liberationis in iisdem computrescant.
english: Thesis XLVIII. 'These preliminary effects, produced in people's minds by the power of the word and Spirit, can be smothered and entirely put out through the fault of a rebellious will, and in many they usually are.

So some people, in whose minds the power of the word and Spirit has stamped a measure of knowledge of divine truth, some grief for their sins, and some longing and concern for deliverance, are turned completely the other way: they reject the truth and hate it, hand themselves over to their desires, grow hardened in their sins, and rot in them with no longing or concern for deliverance.'

source_text: XLIX. Addunt ne electos quidem ipsos in hisce praecedaneis ad regenerationem actibus ita se gerere unquam, quin propter negligentiam & resistentiam suam possint juste a Deo deseri & derelinqui: sed eam esse erga illos specialem Dei misericordiam, ut quamvis hanc gratiam excitantem & illuminantem repellant aliquamdiu, aut suffocent, eos tamen iterum, iterumque urgeat Deus, nec desistat promovere, donec eosdem gratiae suae prorsus subjugaverit, ac in statu filiorum regeneratorum collocaverit.
english: Thesis XLIX. They add that even the elect never behave in these acts that go before regeneration so well that God could not justly abandon and forsake them for their negligence and resistance.

But God's special mercy toward them is such that, though they push away or smother this stirring and enlightening grace for a time, he presses them again and again and does not stop leading them forward until he has brought them wholly under his grace and set them in the state of regenerate children.
